content: In the United Republic of Tanzania, a study was conducted with three treatment groups: a saline bolus group, an albumin bolus group, and a no-bolus group. Children in the saline bolus group received 9% saline solution at a dose of 20 mL per kilogram of body weight over one hour, while those in the albumin bolus group received intravenous albumin solution at the same dose and duration. The comparator group received no bolus fluids. The comparison between saline bolus and no bolus was deemed most relevant for clinical guidelines. Approximately 90% of participants received hypotonic maintenance fluids (5% dextrose). Additional treatments included antimalarial, antipyretic, and anticonvulsant medications, as well as interventions for hypoglycemia and blood transfusions when necessary. If impaired perfusion persisted, additional boluses of 20 mL/kg over one hour were administered. Following a protocol amendment, the initial bolus volume was increased to 40 mL/kg. The rationale for increasing the initial bolus volume was outlined in a commentary on the FEAST trial. First, the original bolus volume of 20 mL/kg may have been insufficient to address the study question. Third, only 1% of trial participants had severe hypotensive shock (compared to the 5% predicted in the trial design), which could have influenced the comparison between saline and albumin boluses. The primary outcome of the trial was mortality 48 hours after randomization, while secondary outcomes included mortality at four weeks, neurological sequelae, episodes of hypotensive shock within 48 hours, and adverse events. Children were followed up for four weeks, and those with neurological impairments were followed up at 24 weeks. Stratum A included 3,141 children aged 60 days to 12 years, with a median age of 23–25 months. Approximately 46–48% were female. Capillary refill time was ≥2 seconds in 64–69% of children and ≥3 seconds in 25–29%. Severe anemia was present in one-third of the children, and about 15% were in a coma. Malaria parasitemia was detected in 58% of participants. Children with severe malnutrition, gastroenteritis, non-infectious causes of shock, or contraindications to volume expansion were excluded. Stratum B included 29 children with severe hypotension. The median age was 21 months in the saline bolus group and 28 months in the albumin bolus group. Girls comprised 50% of the saline bolus group and 38% of the albumin bolus group. Capillary refill time was ≥2 seconds in 8–19% of children and ≥3 seconds in 69–77%. Severe anemia was present in 38% of the saline bolus group and 58% of the albumin bolus group. Coma was observed in 56% and 77% of children in the two groups, respectively. Malaria parasitemia was found in 31% of the saline bolus group and 62% of the albumin bolus group. The FEAST trial demonstrated clear harm associated with rapid intravenous fluid infusions in children with febrile illnesses such as pneumonia, malaria, and meningitis, or those with severe anemia who did not meet the WHO criteria for shock. Adverse outcomes were attributed to fluid overload, including pulmonary edema, heart failure, and cerebral edema, although other mechanisms may have contributed. The trial excluded children with diarrhea and severe dehydration, as well as those with severe acute malnutrition. The updated guidelines emphasize that children with febrile illnesses, severe pneumonia, severe malaria, meningitis, severe acute malnutrition, or severe anemia do not require additional fluids beyond those needed to maintain normal hydration. Rapid intravenous fluid administration in these children can lead to heart failure, lung congestion, cerebral edema, and exacerbation of anemia due to hemodilution. Instead, initial care should focus on identifying the underlying cause of the condition and providing appropriate treatment. The guideline development group (GDG) noted that children presenting with signs of impaired circulation are at risk of clinical deterioration. Full assessment and reassessment of circulatory status are essential to exclude progression to shock or signs of fluid overload. Maintenance fluids should be administered based on age and weight, and intravenous fluids should be given only until the child can tolerate oral fluids. For children in shock, the GDG recommended cautious fluid management. Children with cold extremities, prolonged capillary refill time, and a weak, fast pulse should receive 10–20 mL/kg of isotonic crystalloid fluids over 30–60 minutes, followed by reassessment. If shock persists, a further infusion of 10 mL/kg over 30 minutes may be considered. If shock resolves, only maintenance fluids should be provided. Signs of fluid overload, cardiac failure, or neurological deterioration should prompt immediate cessation of fluid infusions. Children with severe anemia (hemoglobin <5 g/dL) should receive a blood transfusion as early as possible, with other intravenous fluids limited to maintaining normal hydration. In children with severe acute malnutrition, intravenous fluids should be administered cautiously at 10–15 mL/kg over the first hour. If no improvement is observed after one hour, a blood transfusion should be given slowly over at least three hours. The GDG emphasized the importance of training health workers to assess and manage children with shock accurately. In low-resource settings, simple algorithms and adequate training are essential to guide emergency management. Access to oxygen, pulse oximetry, and other forms of respiratory support can significantly influence outcomes. Children with severe anemia should receive blood transfusions promptly, but practical challenges in low-resource settings may delay this intervention. The GDG concluded that fluid therapy alone may not suffice for managing many children in shock. Early inotropic or ventilator support may be required.
